profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional hospital network is exploring how to adapt the KCPS (knowledgeable creative problem-solving) approach into a repeatable internal innovation format for frontline staff. This brainstorming meeting is between the Innovation Office and the Knowledge Management team, and the immediate context is a planned pilot focused on generating ideas to reduce nurse time spent searching for supplies during night shifts. The agenda is to sketch what a KCPS-inspired pilot should look like, what kind of knowledge should be made available to participants, and what outputs the team should expect from the first run. The expected outcome is a rough shared plan for the pilot structure, supporting materials, and how ideas will be captured for review.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Design thinking workshops, service design, frontline process improvement
members.background: Elena previously ran rapid ideation programs at two hospital innovation labs and now leads short-format improvement workshops for clinical operations teams.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to be lightweight enough to launch within a month using existing facilitation materials, without creating dependency on a new platform or a large preparation burden for busy clinical staff.
hidden_assumptions: Knowledge provision in a brainstorming setting mainly means giving participants a concise pre-curated packet of examples, constraints, and relevant facts before or at the start of the session.
In an early-stage creativity pilot, a 'concept' can be a brief but distinct idea direction captured as a title, sketch, and one-line explanation.
When people say 'the workshop' or 'the pilot session,' they usually mean the live facilitated meeting itself, not the surrounding prep and synthesis work.
If someone suggests using the existing 'case-study template,' the obvious reference is the Innovation Office's one-page concept card used in prior ideation sessions.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Knowledge repositories, evidence packaging, enterprise taxonomy, clinical information workflows
members.background: Ravi is a former medical librarian who now manages the hospital network's knowledge systems and helps operational teams turn dispersed institutional know-how into reusable decision support.
members.private_state: He wants this pilot to demonstrate that the organization's underused knowledge assets can actively support creative work, which would strengthen the case for expanding the internal knowledge portal.
hidden_assumptions: Knowledge provision is most valuable when participants can retrieve targeted internal examples, policy snippets, and evidence on demand during idea generation rather than only receiving a fixed packet upfront.
A concept is not really countable unless it is documented enough to show context, operating principle, and what knowledge informed it.

A proper KCPS-style workshop includes the surrounding activities where participants contribute prompts beforehand and where outputs are synthesized afterward, because that is part of how knowledge gets transformed.

If someone proposes using the standard 'case-study template,' the default reference is the Quality Office's improvement case-study form that records background, intervention logic, stakeholders, and expected impact.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the pilot needs strong 'knowledge provision' to support creativity.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means a tightly curated starter pack prepared in advance: a few observed pain points, examples from other units, and known constraints handed to participants before ideation begins.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means live access to a searchable collection of internal cases, policy excerpts, and prior improvement notes that participants can query while generating ideas.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds technical but shared, and both approaches plausibly fit the article's language, so each hears confirmation of their own interpretation without needing clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as '10-12 concepts' from the pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say it would be good if the pilot produced 'around a dozen concepts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means roughly 10-12 distinct idea directions emerging from the live session, even if each is only captured as a sketch or headline concept.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means 10-12 documented concept entries with enough structure to indicate rationale, use context, and supporting knowledge sources, similar to a mini case record.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They appear aligned on the same number and on being ambitious but realistic; the hidden difference is the threshold for what qualifies as one countable concept, which is easy to leave implicit in brainstorming.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'the workshop' or 'the pilot'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to keep the first pilot 'to one workshop next month.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena treats the workshop as the single 90-minute live session, with any prep emails or later write-up considered peripheral logistics rather than part of the pilot itself.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi treats the workshop as the whole intervention package: a short pre-session knowledge prompt, the live session, and a structured post-session synthesis step to convert ideas into reusable knowledge.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In everyday work talk, 'workshop' often casually stands in for the entire initiative, so the scope difference feels too ordinary to interrogate unless scheduling pressure exposes it later.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'case-study template' they plan to reuse
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they can 'reuse the case-study template' so the pilot does not start from scratch.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the Innovation Office's one-page concept card used in prior design sprints, with fields for idea name, quick sketch, user need, and possible next step.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi is thinking of the Quality Office's improvement case-study form, which asks for current-state summary, evidence basis, workflow implications, and implementation notes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both templates are known internally and both are casually called 'the case-study template,' so neither participant notices they are mentally pointing to different default artifacts.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this pilot light and runnable with what we already use. If we can frame it as one 90-minute live session next month, I can pull together a simple brief, facilitate it, and avoid turning this into a big infrastructure project. For this stage, the point is to get clinicians in a room, spark ideas quickly, and not burden them with a lot of prep.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. For the night-shift supply-search problem, I'd love for us to shape this as a lightweight KCPS-inspired pilot and keep the first pass to one workshop next month. If we can make it manageable for frontline staff, I think we'll get a cleaner read on whether the format has legs.

turns.inner_thought: One workshop next month is fine as long as we treat the pilot as the full package, not just the live meeting. This is a good opportunity to show that our knowledge assets can actively support creative work. The key is strong knowledge provision so people aren't limited to whatever examples they happen to remember in the room.
turns.utterance: I agree. And I think this is a good use case because it lets us build in real knowledge provision, so people aren't just ideating from memory or from the loudest anecdote in the room. If we do that well, the pilot should be much more grounded.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—I'll assemble a concise starter packet with a few examples from other units, the main pain points we've already heard, and practical constraints like staffing, storage rules, and night coverage. That should be enough to orient people without asking them to learn a system or do homework.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's how I was thinking about it too. We could open with a short packet that lays out a few examples from other units, the common supply-search pain points, and the main constraints, so everyone starts with the right knowledge in front of them.

turns.inner_thought: A starter packet is useful, but the stronger move is to let participants retrieve what they need during ideation—internal cases, policy fragments, prior notes, whatever becomes relevant as different directions emerge. That's the kind of knowledge provision that would demonstrate the portal's value. I'll phrase it as an extension of her point so it sounds aligned.
turns.utterance: That makes sense, and I think we can build on it. Alongside that, it would be great if people could also pull relevant internal cases and policy snippets during the session as part of the knowledge provision layer, so the conversation can stay responsive as ideas evolve.

turns.inner_thought: As long as we don't overcomplicate it, fine. What I really care about is leaving the live session with a healthy spread of viable idea directions—maybe a dozen rough concepts on boards or cards. If we get that many distinct directions in 90 minutes, I'll call the pilot a success.
turns.utterance: Right. For me, the pilot will feel successful if we can leave the room with around a dozen concepts—something in the spirit of the article's case study output, where you can see several different directions rather than just one or two polished answers.

turns.inner_thought: A dozen is a sensible target if they're documented properly. I need each concept to be countable as a concept entry, not just a sticky-note headline—there should be enough there to preserve context, rationale, and what knowledge informed it. Otherwise we can't reuse the outputs or show the value of the knowledge layer.
turns.utterance: I like that target too. Around a dozen concepts feels ambitious but realistic, and it would be especially valuable if each one is captured in a way that preserves what knowledge informed it so we can review and reuse them afterward.

turns.inner_thought: No need to create new paperwork. We already have the Innovation Office concept card from prior ideation sessions—title, sketch, user need, next step. That's plenty for early-stage concepts and keeps facilitation simple.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And I don't think we need to invent the documentation from scratch here—we can just reuse the case-study template the team already has, which should be enough to capture the outputs without slowing people down.

turns.inner_thought: Good, the Quality Office form should work well. It already fits how improvement knowledge is stored, and if we use it, the post-session synthesis will be straightforward. That also helps position this pilot as part of a broader knowledge workflow rather than a one-off brainstorm.
turns.utterance: Yes, reusing the case-study template should help a lot. It will make the post-session synthesis easier and keep the pilot aligned with how improvement knowledge is normally stored, which is a big plus if we want this to be repeatable.

turns.inner_thought: I need to anchor this back to a simple 90-minute live format before it balloons. My plan is brief framing, a fast round of idea generation, then share-outs and clustering. If we keep momentum high, we can still get 10 to 12 concept directions without exhausting clinicians.
turns.utterance: So in terms of flow, I'd keep it very simple: quick framing, idea generation, then concept sharing, all within about 90 minutes. If we can do that cleanly, I think one workshop next month stays realistic and doesn't overload the clinicians.

turns.inner_thought: That live format is fine, and I'll make sure the broader workshop package includes a short prompt beforehand plus a consolidation step afterward. That's where a lot of the knowledge transformation actually happens. If I can secure those bookends, this pilot can produce reusable knowledge as well as ideas and support the case for expanding the portal.
turns.utterance: That format sounds workable to me. And if we gather prompts beforehand and do a short consolidation afterward, the workshop should generate reusable knowledge as well as ideas, which would make the pilot much more valuable on our side too.
